abstract.text:
Abstract—The static voltage stability studies of the AC system 
with VSC-HVDC (Voltage Source Converter-based High Voltage 
Direct Current) connected renewable energy mainly focus on 
reactive power control. This paper proposes a coordinated active 
and reactive power control strategy based on the L -index to 
improve the static voltage stability of the receiving-end AC system. 
Firstly, for a power system including the VSC-HVDC connected 
renewable energy , the L -index and its sensitivity to different 
variables are calculated. Secondly, an optimization model for 
coordinated control of the VSC -HVDC connected renewable 
energy is established  by using  the L -index of the receiving -end 
system as the optimization objective, and power flow, node voltage, 
and transmission power as co nstraints. Finally, the optimization 
model is solved using the Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) 
algorithm to obtain the optimal active and reactive power support 
values. Simulation results show that the coordinated control 
method can significantly improve the static voltage stability of the 
receiving-end AC system while ensuring the safe operation of the 
system.

introduction.text:
I. INTRODUCTION  
With the implementation of the "dual carbon" goals, the 
proportion of renewable energy has increased significantly. 
Flexible DC transmission technology, with its advantages in 
integrating renewable energy, has become an important 
component of modern power systems. However, this also poses 
greater challenges to system voltage stability [1-3]. In normal 
working conditions, the onshore converter station lacks active 
response and support for grid voltage disturbances, and the 
dynamic response capabilities for active and reactive power of 
the flexible DC system cannot be fully utilized [4]. Therefore, it 
is essential to propose a coordinated active and reactive power 
control strategy for the  power system including the VSC-HVDC 
connected renewable energy . 
Static voltage stability is an important indicator for 
measuring the ability of a power system to maintain stable 
voltage levels under normal operating conditions. The main 
research methods for static voltage stability include the 
continuation power flow method [5], sensitivity analysis [6], 
eigenvalue analysis [7], singular value analysis [8], L index, and 
artificial intelligence methods [9]. Among these methods, the L 
index is widely used due to its fast computation speed, clear 
physical meaning, and sensitivity to parameter changes. 
Reference[10] combined power flow equations to propose the 
sensitivity of the L index to load and the relationship between 
the L index and eigenvalues, and based on this, pointed out 
methods to determine the threshold of the L index. Reference[11] 
proposed an improved PEM to calculate the moments and semi-
invariants of the L index for calculating voltage instability risk. 
Reference[12] constructed a static voltage stability assessment 
model based on the L index using extended affine arithmetic, 
and then quantitatively evaluated the importance of each 
variable's impact on static voltage stability. Although the above 
references have reasonably assessed the static voltage stability 
performance based on the L index, they are all limited to AC 
systems and rarely consider the impact of renewable energy 
integration via VSC-HVDC. 
Currently, research on the static voltage stability of a power 
system including the VSC-HVDC connected renewable energy 
mostly focuses on reactive power. Reference[13] uses the 
Jacobian matrix at the system voltage collapse point to derive 
the sensitivity of the system load margin to VSC-HVDC control 
parameters. It prioritizes adjusting the parameters with higher 
sensitivity to enhance static voltage stability. Reference[14 ] 
identifies critical nodes and lines in AC/DC hybrid systems 
through modal analysis and improves the overall system's static 
voltage stability by providing reactive power compensation to This work was supported by the Science & Technology Project of SGCC 
(Research on frequency and voltage support for deep-sea wind power 
integrated through VSC-HVDC system, 4000-202318465A-3-2-ZN).

these nodes or lines. Reference[15] establishes an optimization 
model with voltage deviation, L index, active power loss, and 
total reactive power compensation as optimization objectives to 
solve the reactive power compensation capacity for offshore 
wind power integration via VSC-HVDC systems. It can be seen 
that the primary focus of all the above references is given to the 
optimization of  reactive power compensation, neglecting the 
contribution from active power regulation of the converter 
stations, which will be shown in the paper to play a significant 
role in system static voltage stability as well.  
In light of the shortcomings of previous research, this paper 
proposes a coordinated active and reactive power control 
strategy based on the L index. Firstly, for a power system 
including the VSC -HVDC connected renewable energy , the L 
index and its sensitivity to different variables  are calculated 
based on the power flow equations, and the renewable energy 
integration via VSC-HVDC is modeled as a power source. Then, 
an optimization model for coordinated control of the VSC -
HVDC connected renewable energy is established . The 
optimization model is solved using the PSO algorithm to obtain 
the optimal active and reactive power support capacities. Finally, 
the effectiveness of the proposed coordinated control method are 
verified in a model containing a VSC-HVDC system.

conclusion.text:
V. CONCLUSION 
This paper proposes a coordinated active and reactive power 
control strategy for VSC-HVDC connected renewable energy  
to improve system static voltage stability represented by the L 
index. The sensitivity of L index to different variables are 
theoretically explained and validated through simulations , 
presenting a calculation error that is less than 3% . Compared 
with the methods providing only active power support, the 
proposed coordinated control strategy can improve the L index 
by almost 25% . Compared with the methods providing only 
reactive power support, the proposed strategy can not only 
better enhance the L index  but also ensure that the system's 
voltage is within the safety limit. Comprehensive case studies 
have demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed control 
strategy in improving system voltage stability. In the future, the 
impact of the coordinated control strategy on other voltage 
stability indexes will be investigated.
